I played the Bioshock games in order of release. I played BS1 when it first came out, then I fell out of touch with the series for a bit. By the time BSI came out, I decided I should catch up and play BS2 first, then Infinite. BS1 and BS2 are great games and I would recommend them to almost anyone. BSI is... different. There's something about it that I'm just not getting into. Part of it could be the level design, which is actually rather linear even though the levels look cosmetically "wide open". Part of it could be the limited vigors and even more straightforward shoot-and-kill gameplay. I found the entire game so far to veer wildly between extremely easy and "multiple deaths before you even figure out the level's geometry" difficult. Most grunt battles are insignificant and tedious. Most boss battles appear to require at least one death just to figure out the parameters. After a few unavoidable resurrection cutscenes, you're back in the fray again. After a few more, Bioshock Infinite throws in a smug little message about how you can change the difficulty at any time. I nearly lost all forward momentum through the game during a boss battle. Later, I'm at a ghost and I've gotten stuck. I can't stay alive long enough to figure out the fight's tactics for myself, and I don't care enough about the alternate-history background, or the riddle of the Statue, or the mystery of the character's history to keep plugging away at the same boss battle. The voice actor is especially grating. How this game, and not the first or second, is the best-known title of the series is a mystery to me. Probably because of superficial appeal.

That's a good thought provoking post, but I think it's forwarding a niche viewpoint by relying on very outlier commentary. But let's break down a few elements. A certain political figure is a political sideliner, given the fall of his father (which I personally remember as an observer). Obviously Chinese politics doesn't have a "liberal" wing in the same sense that Western democracies do, but the closest analog might be the reformist wing. This political wing would have a vested interest in emphasizing aspects of the Chinese government which lean towards totalitarianism and so forth, and conversely the main arm of the Chinese government would likely keep this wing under increased political pressure, similar to other critics who have spoken out against the government. (This is regardless of the objective *merit* of his opinions.) A well-known whistleblower is under very similar such pressures from the U.S. government. But neither individual is particularly representative of that government's general treatment of its mainstream citizenry. A major international newspaper has a well-deserved reputation for investigative journalism often at odds with those in power - whether in the US or China. I would also emphasize that the newspaper's commitment to reporting facts inconvenient to the Chinese gov't has traditionally put it at direct odds with the gov't. Controls have waxed and waned over the years - there was a period during a previous leadership when the newspaper was allowed past the internet censorship, although no longer. Journalists also routinely get harassed by gov't minders. Within the Chinese apparatus, foreign press workers are also undoubtedly in the "tightly watched" circles, similar to disgraced reformers. This doesn't invalidate their critiques of the Chinese government, but it does address how their experience and viewpoint will be very different from the average Chinese citizen's, or the average foreigner in China's. The article you linked to appears to be a highly-optimized search result from Google concerning China and the fascism question, but let's take a closer look at its timing. It was written in 2012, which was during or shortly after a leadership handover of power. At the time of publication, China was in the middle of a leadership change - press controls have always been tighter during these periods in a way that they generally are not once the leader has been secured. Also, the article cites to a speech from 2005 by that political figure... referring to the deposement of his father in 1987. 2005 puts us only a year or so into a new administration. And 1987 puts us back into the communes, planned economy, and on the other side of a famous police action in 1989. Things have changed. But to get at your main question of "is China a fascist police state?" The simplest approach might be to look at definitions, rather than a 3-year-old article from a news source the Chinese government historically dislikes, citing a decade-old speech by a political exile, referring to a deposement from 30 years ago. An economic encyclopedia defines fascism (economically) as "socialism with a capitalist veneer" which certainly looks promising. But further down, in the detailed overview, it elaborates:  > "Where socialism sought totalitarian control of a society’s economic processes through direct state operation of the means of production, fascism sought that control indirectly, through domination of nominally private owners. Where socialism nationalized property explicitly, fascism did so implicitly, by requiring owners to use their property in the “national interest”—that is, as the autocratic authority conceived it. (Nevertheless, a few industries were operated by the state.) Where socialism abolished all market relations outright, fascism left the appearance of market relations while planning all economic activities. Where socialism abolished money and prices, fascism controlled the monetary system and set all prices and wages politically. In doing all this, fascism denatured the marketplace. Entrepreneurship was abolished. State ministries, rather than consumers, determined what was produced and under what conditions." China has some of these elements today, and it pointedly lacks several others: * **domination of nominally private owners?** Debatable. Big business owners are encouraged to join the ruling party, and since a political doctrine from the late 90s, they have had a seat at the table as one of three classes of socialist heroes. The government still maintains state-owned enterprises, but is trying to restructure most of them along competitive models. Private entrepreneurs do not typically receive assignments from the government (though the usual admin work of tax reports and stock declarations exist). * **requiring owners to use their property in the "national interest"?** As above, the government does not assign or give orders to private enterprise, beyond rising procedural concerns such as environmental protection and tax dodging. The government does not, for example, tell a major car manufacturer what model of car to make, or whom to sell it to, or which factory's raw materials to use. * **left the appearance of market relations while planning all economic activities?** Regarding the SOEs and the state banks, this charge has some merit to it. Chinese economic planners declare monthly or annual target numbers (and, somewhat contrivedly, always seem to meet them). But outside of the SOEs and the state banking sector (including a major privately held bank) there are no direct macroeconomic controls imposed by the state upon private enterprise. * **control the monetary system, setting all prices and wages politically?** No. The Chinese government holds reserves of goods and sets central banking interest rates, and can manipulate these to try to sway prices the way they want (usually to avoid disastrous inflation of the sort that triggered the 1989 protests), but this is a far cry from setting prices and wages. This is also nothing to with its controls over ForEx rates. * **Entrepreneurship was abolished?** Absolutely not. The opposite is true (see the political doctrine, as well as the numerous "New High Tech zones" in almost every major city, with incubators to promote sci-tech.) This is nothing like the PRC of the 1950s or the USSR of the 1920s. * **State ministries, rather than consumers, determined what was produced and under what conditions?** No, if anything, the Chinese government has been trying desperately to boost domestic consumption ever since growth dropped below 8% at around 2011 and foreign direct investment/foreign exports took a hit. Other factors from that site: * **Interventionism seeks to guide the market process, not eliminate it, as fascism did.** China's government is absolutely trying to co-opt the free market process, after decades of trying to eliminate it. Not a fascist economy. * **Under fascism, the state, through official cartels, controlled all aspects of manufacturing, commerce, finance, and agriculture.** This is no longer the case in China, as its SOEs only make up a portion of the industry and the rest are private enterprise. * **Planning boards set product lines, production levels, prices, wages, working conditions, and the size of firms.** Not the case. * **Levels of consumption were dictated by the state, and “excess” incomes had to be surrendered as taxes or “loans.”** Not the case. There are a couple of elements that could apply to China: * "To maintain high employment and minimize popular discontent, fascist governments also undertook massive public-works projects financed by steep taxes, borrowing, and fiat money creation. While many of these projects were domestic—roads, buildings, stadiums—the largest project of all was militarism, with huge armies and arms production." The 'massive public works projects' part absolutely applies, although the 'steep taxes' and 'fiat money creation' bits less so. The army part is a special case - China has generally had a numerically huge armed force, and it is indeed spending heavily on it currently, but the primary focus appears to shrink its headcount and refine it to a more advanced modern force (and most experts agree it will be many decades before it even draws level with the U.S. armed forces in quality). So much for the economic aspects of fascism, which I think have a few similar colors to China but which ultimately fall wide of the mark (primarily, they fail to take into account China's continuing divestment of the SOEs and its increasing reliance on entrepreneurs from major tech companies and other private enterprise). I then wanted to start looking into political definitions of fascism, and then I got lost down a very deep rabbit hole of competing discussions of this. I may pick back up from here if I get a more clear picture - but for now I don't have a good enough handle of the current thinking behind the political definition to comment. One other dimension which could be worth investigating in a later discussion is to what extent China is a "police state", since that was present in your initial description (but less so in the newspaper article later linked).

I'm actually reading through the King James Bible right now on an electronic device. Incidentally I'm reading it right after reading several histories of China. It's fascinating how similar the first few chapters are, even between Mediterranean basin and Yellow/Yangtze River civilizations. They're both works that follow a utilitarian message of "Here are my laws, but first, this is why you should listen to me because I'm descended from a deity". Part 1: Here's our version of how an omnipotent deity created the universe as we know it. One of the first things is to separate sky from the surface (both God and China's Pangu had to do this). Part 2: Genealogies! Your king, who paid me to write this, is descended from these deities (whether God or Huangdi) via a convoluted ancestry which you won't question because you probably can't read. Many of these will follow a chant or sing song pattern for verbal memorization and verbal transmission through the ages. Note that we will not fill out every single branch of the family tree, because leaving a few blank means we can retcon future important rulers and powerful converts into it. Seriously, if we can convert a neighboring king by conveniently discovering that he's a lesser cousin of our divinity then can you imagine how much that would save on armies and fighting? But the ones who won't submit we can defeat first and then ascribe their failure to divine reasons like failure to follow proper ritual. Part 3: Now that we've established that the deity created everything and is omnipotent and is directly responsible for how people behave, we're going to tell many tales of this same deity behaving in an oddly parochial and xenophobic style, favoring one particular family life and behaving much less like Father of All and much more like Ancestral Protective Spirit. This deity is not concerned with women or people outside your family, except where they further the main goal of reproduction. Both cultures reserve the Curse of Barrenness (Abram's assailants in Egypt, Mengzi's caution to vile criminals) as its most virulent curse for the worst offenders. You are to reproduce and multiply above all other concerns, even the sustainable welfare of your resources and environment. We'll record schisms and exiles of key figures due to overpopulation but we won't admit that this was caused by the policy of  "children first" in any way. Caveat. We will not address how, exactly, a foreign tribe that is satisfyingly and bloodily defeated was in any way not directly created by the same deity that claims responsibility for all of creation. This is just another wrinkle in the post facto conversion of our deity from a nomadic tribal ancestral totem, to a cosmogenical higher power that is omnipotent, omniscient, and omnipresent. It's a fascinating read, especially from a viewpoint of societal needs and anthropology. The priorities of survival in a brutal environment above all else (and the post facto justifications for extreme actions, e.g. Lot's incest with his two daughters to procreate) are very plain. I'm looking forward to the New Testament though, as I hear that has much more of a philosophical inquiry to it than the "God as overprotective jealous parent" chronicle of the OT.

In the Old Testament specifically, there is a very strong focus on fathering children, especially sons. Many mentions of women focus solely on their fertility and how many sons they bore for the patriarch. Even a low status handmaiden could be promoted if she bore a son to the patriarch. Given the context of the Old Testament's location, this focus on masculine tribal birth rates may be understandable. Even a peaceful life is hard, given the inhospitable terrain and subsistence herding or harvesting, which rely on male strength to break the ground for planting or to handle the animal stock (goats and donkeys are often mentioned as high status stock, and they are not docile or small enough for children or women to handle as easily as men). Add in the fact that life was often violent, with theft, deception, and murder often occurring as fiat means of settling disputes, and it's clear that sons are essential in a tribe's survival. The ability to field fighting-age males is a deterrent to theft and violence, quite separate from their strength in the field in times of peace. So you have a culture that is extremely focused on producing male children, more or less above any other form of individual contribution. A man is not only regarded for the work he can do and the fights he can win in his lifetime, but also is judged on the contribution he makes to posterity - the value of the fruit of his loins. A homosexual individual thus represents a grave opportunity cost by possibly eliminating a whole lineage of male descendants. In a culture where every pair of strong hands helps to perpetuate your clan, a person who opts not to reproduce might be seen as a short sighted freeloader.  Consider the example of Onan, for example, who is required to have sex with a woman who is not his chosen partner, and he "spills his seed on the ground" (later taken to mean masturbation, but it could have been withdrawal or interruptus or any number of other practices). He is cursed because he avoided an act that could have caused impregnation, and that is such a perverse dereliction of duty that the Old Testament holds him worthy of punishment. (Interestingly, the OT seems to be generally quiet about female homosexuality. There is one chapter dedicated to a handmaiden who intentionally seduced a patriarch into having sex with her while he thought she was a non local stranger prostitute, and then obtained a personal item from him proving their liaison and afterwards compelled him to recognize the child she bears him - the narrative has no particular criticism of her actions and even seems to legitimize her child as part of the clan through the mother's machinations.)

I used to think the victory points rewards for a complex space-themed board game were piddling little drops in the bucket, but now I'm thinking they may be just as important as board position. Edit: the Space Race gives up to 13 VPs if you progress on it fully and your opponent progresses zero. If your opponent progresses along it entirely after you, they get something like 4 points, for 9 net in your favor. This is maybe equivalent to absolutely controlling a non European region in the game, maybe a bit less. Space Race also immediately lets you safely get rid of cards that could instantly lose you the game. It also gives you some special powers that last until the enemy attains the same Space Race track. In my opinion, Space Race is slightly harder to pursue strategically as one faction than as the other, since so many cards would cause DEFCON suicide and you need to keep Space Race cards for them. But the VPs are actually not a bad return on card OP values, and some of the powers are really nice in practice. The ability to see the enemy headline first, or to discard a held card, both remove very real sources of DEFCON suicide from the game. I've played probably two to three hundred games of this board game from a long time ago to now and I'm still learning new things about it. I used to think the Space Race was a complete waste of time but now that I've been exposed to a specific playstyle, I'm holding it in more of a grudging regard.

Yeah, the concept of "central territory" frankly had less to do with an ethnicity or kingdom and more to do with the idea of "here's fertile agricultural land - now everybody wants to take and hold it for posterity". A large Asian country was for many centuries a shifting land of borders and minor kingdoms, but one constant was that everybody was trying to deal with the rush to the middle. To the north and west, there was hostile dry desert territory, hard to eke out a living on. To the east was endless sea, and to the south was increasingly hostile jungle, hard to subdue and colonize (though they tried, for a long time - the dethroned emperors frequently fled to neighboring countries). From the first emperor - himself a western foreigner from the far extreme of a specific geographic loop - through the Mongolian rulers of various dynasties, to the final Manchurian rulers of the Qing - even far flung invaders coveted the territory and would risk violence and disorder to claim it. The Chinese sense of cultural superiority and being the center of the world was most famously encountered in the last dynasty, the Qing dynasty, when it dealt with the resurgent European powers. But it had its origins in millennia of struggle for the cradle of East Asian civilization, in a fertile plain and river valley framed by major rivers, and which simple population pressures forced dynasty after dynasty to vie for control over. The administrative struggles of ruling an agrarian empire, at many times comprising the largest by contemporary population, made it rare for a Chinese emperor to care much about what was beyond their borders.

Tibetan culture had centuries of interaction with Chinese culture - in fact, some linguists posit that the current Putonghua dialect development had more Tibetan sources than native "Chinese" (whatever that may mean - it's a slippery definition). So "China" isn't really a tribe of people in an ethnic sense. It also didn't start off as a single kingdom or polity or other entity. It started off as a place - the "central lands" or "central state" of prosperous, rich agricultural lands which seasonally flooded. It spurred the development of a centralized administration to manage the water resources, and it attracted many peoples from the surrounding regions once it became clear exactly how abundant a population the two riversheds (Yellow River/Huang He and Yangzi River/Chang Jiang) could sustain. If you imagine China more as a central plain territory ringed by these rivers, able to sustain a stable population, and hotly sought after for its resources, this may be a more accurate way of thinking about it through its historical development. If you take the Shang Dynasty as the first fully historical dynasty (the prior Xia Dynasty did leave written records, but they were quasi mythical and spiritual), then you've got maybe 2,600 years of continuous inhabitation, and competition, and striving and strife to control and own the prosperous central territory. To the east is salt water seas, to the south is hills and mountains and eventually jungles, to the west is desert and mountains, and to the north likewise. So that's the Chinese - who are less of a race or ethnicity or unified tribe of people, and more just a collection of genetically diverse folks who happen to be in and around this area. When China calls itself the Middle Kingdom, it's not a self-aggrandizement, or denigrating other regions of the world. Rather, the emphasis is more on the central vital importance that the Chinese region played on the lives of those living there. China as the Middle Kingdom is foremost a geographic concept, like "Mediterranean" originally meant "center land" in the West. So those are the Chinese, or at least the geographic definition of the proto tribes who eventually coalesced, conquered, exterminated, interbred, unified, and built up into modern China. But who are the Tibetans? Tibet is geographically at the western extreme of this "Middle Kingdom" schema. Tibet is high altitude, with less agricultural plant yields and a far greater emphasis on livestock. Tibet also was more accessible to trade with the Indus Valley (similarly, those who later unified and became the Indian civilization from a collection of tribes and kindgoms) as well as the trading Central Asian peoples. Tibet had linguistic interactions with the Chinese, and even in Imperial Chinese times, there were special Tibetan delegation quarters in Chinese cities (as is still visible in modern Beijing). Buddhism apparently arrived in China at least twice, first by sea, with relatively little cultural effect, and then once overland some time later via Tibet and India. By this time, Tibetan culture assimilated some of the Buddhist teachings and its priesthood (Lamas) became important social office holders, eventually constituting the ruling class. Buddhism was slower to permeate the Chinese political ranks (which had been made up of a combination of Confucianist and Daoist practitioners, along with a large and evolving pantheon of traditional Chinese gods). One of the first Imperial rulers to fully support Buddhism, in fact, was Wu Zetian, the first and to date only female Emperor, who faced such opposition from the patriarchal Confucian society that she went outside her own ruling class religions, and embraced the lower-class religion of Buddhism to make up her power base. Culturally, Buddhist teachings in China have always stressed a paradise to the west of a land of riches (likely India) to be reached only through arduous journeys over the Himalayas and through Tibet. So that is one major cultural dealing between the two regions. The Tibetan ruling structure had historically been quite distinct from the Chinese Imperial rule, and as Chinese emperors and dynasties came and went, their dealings with Tibet varied. At worst, Tibet constituted an unfriendly peripheral culture that proved a military opponent (perhaps similar to the Mongols, Xiongnu, Huns, Turkics, Manchurians, etc. etc.). At best, Tibetan rulers accepted a place within the Chinese order, similar to a suzerainty arrangement, where internal local affairs were handled by their own rulers, but broader affairs deferred to the Emperor. The final Chinese dynasty, the Qing Dynasty, was ethnically not the majority Han Chinese at all - they were Manchurians from the northeast of China who overthrew the Ming Dynasty and proved militarily very capable. They also were fortunate enough to have relatively stable and long-lived heirs in quick succession, in the Kangxi, Yongzheng*, and Qianlong Emperors (each man ruling for many decades, across three successive generations). These rulers pushed the northern frontier back against the Orthodox Russian Empire, the Korean peninsula back against Japanese neighbors, and even expanded towards southeast Asia. (cont. below) edit: wrong name of a Qing emperor

However, after about three centuries of Qing rule, later emperors were inept and weak. Britain came to the Indus Valley and forcibly united the colonized Raj (which later fragmented into India, Pakistan, and Bangladesh - formerly East Pakistan - after the British departed) and then turned its opposition to Russia, competing for control over Central Asia. Tibet was a key region during this "Great Game" era, and Britain's strategy required Tibet to stay neutral. If Russia could gain access to Tibet, it would have a long and hostile border with the British dominion across unforgiving territory to threaten British interests there. Britain accordingly executed a treaty with the ailing Qing Dynasty, recognizing Chinese control over Tibet. As has been discussed above, this "control" historically was a much more nebulous and variable thing - at times direct control in fact, at other times a more soft-power client-state style influence of a distant fealty kingdom. Fast forward to the collapse of the Qing Dynasty, the withdrawal of the British from an independent India, and the collapse of Tsarist Russia into the eventual Soviet Union. China's own painful throes were legendary during this time: the Qing Imperial rule was abolished in favor of a Republic in 1912. The Republic's president, a political figure, ill-advisedly attempted to name himself Emperor and was immediately abandoned by his entire Parliament. The Republic's peripheries fell to feuding warlords, whose struggles lasted long enough for some of them to pass their fiefdoms on to a second generation. German, Russian, US, British, French, Portuguese, and Japanese forces carved out colonies along the coast and waited to see whether and how a centralized Chinese government would emerge to finally grant trade concessions. You may have seen the Republic's map of China. It is still used occasionally by the Nationalist Chinese politicians in a neighboring region. Note how it lays claim to not only Tibet, but also Mongolia, and several smaller border areas around Xinjiang and north of Manchuria which are now held by USSR/Russia. The Nationalist Part of China laid claim to all territories held by the Qing Dynasty (which was geographically the largest territory ever held by a Chinese political administration). I'll skip over the Chinese Civil War, which was an even more complex and messy affair. Suffice it to say, the Nationalists and Communists fought against each other, then held a brief ceasefire to fight the Japanese invasion, and finally resumed their fight. As you know, the Communist Chinese won. The Communist victory (or perhaps more accurately, the Nationalist collapse) occurred in several stages, starting from the capture of Beiping (later renamed Beijing) and Tianjin in the north, then through a campaign across the great plain down to the Yangzi River, and finally crossing the Yangzi River and pushing the Nationalists to evacuate to an island. The Communists gained their control over Chinese territories bit by bit, often having to fight the Nationalists and deal with the local powerbrokers to do so. Tibet by that time had been beyond direct control, practically speaking, of the Chinese government for some time. The Communists focussed on Tibet and other outlying regions such as Hainan Island almost immediately after their 1949 victory over the Nationalists. This was important to assert the validity of Communist control and authority over China internally, and also to assert the borders and line-of-control claimed by China as a nation on the international stage. By that time, Chinese Communism had complex and very non-traditional outlooks on economy, social order, manufacturing, etc. that often put it at odds even with other communist nations and with its Soviet ally. Many landlords, scholars, former wealthy classes, etc. which represented the "old corrupt society" were violently dispossessed and cast down, to reform a new model of Chinese society. Tibet, being not only a class-based hierarchy, but a religious one at that, was doubly abhorrent to the new communist order. Modern China (Communist China) incorporated Tibet in 1950 after political negotiations and a series of military actions in which the Chinese forces overcame Tibetan military defenses. A final agreement was made for Tibetan suzerainty, whereby Tibet was recognized as an autonomous region within China, taking its internal affairs under political control, but China's government would represent the region internationally. In 1959, Tibetan military forces attempted an uprising against Chinese rule, which was quashed and which resulted in the Dalai Lama, one of the major spiritual and political leaders of Tibetan society, fleeing to India. Western commentators, especially the British, have strongly criticized Chinese actions in Tibet, including allegations of sustained human rights abuses in Tibet and desecration of Tibetan religion. The Chinese respond that the action resulted in the liberation of Tibetan civilians from a theocratic feudal rule, and that Chinese investments and trade and cultural interchange have brought an increased standard of life to Tibetan people. Today, Tibet receives significant trade, subsidies, and investments from the Chinese central government, while also operating under restrictions in travel to and from the region with close government and police observation.
